enrichment.short_title: Carrier bailment liability for delivery without bills of lading

statutes_considered.title: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1992

key_facts: East West Corporation and Utaniko Limited shipped container loads from Hong Kong to San Antonio, Chile, via Maersk Line and P&O Nedlloyd.
The goods were delivered to Gold Crown without presentation of original bills of lading after the Chilean banks had been sent endorsed bills to collect payment.
Thomas J held the carriers liable for about $230,000 in losses; the carriers appealed on contract, bailment, and bill of lading exemption grounds.
The Court of Appeal upheld liability on bailment and reversionary proprietary interest grounds, not contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a High Court trial judgment holding liner carriers liable for wrongful delivery of goods.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the carriers remained liable, though on reasoning differing in part from the judge below.
enrichment.ratio: Shipowners who deliver cargo without requiring presentation of original bills of lading breach duties owed in bailment, or on an analogous basis, to owners who retained immediate possession or a reversionary proprietary interest; contractual exemption clauses in combined transport bills did not protect the carriers against that breach.
legal_issues: Whether shippers could sue carriers in contract after endorsing bills to collecting banks
Whether owners retained rights in bailment after parting with bills of lading
Whether a reversionary proprietary interest supported a claim for permanent deprivation of goods
Whether bill of lading exemption clauses applied to delivery without presentation of bills

confidence.notes: Outcome, reasoning, and key facts are clearly stated in the Court of Appeal conclusions. Source metadata lists many historical judges not appearing in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Compulsory purchase, adverse possession, and deed poll validity
key_facts: Rhondda Cynon Taff Borough Council compulsorily purchased land from Mr Watkins in the 1960s, entered possession, and was ousted by him in March 1966; he remained on the land for decades.
Compensation was assessed in 1977 and a vesting deed poll was executed in February 1988 after payment into court.
The council brought possession proceedings in 2000; Mr Watkins defended on limitation and public law grounds, alleging the council had abandoned the original open-space purpose.
HHJ Moseley granted summary judgment for possession; Neuberger J dismissed the appeal but suspended the order pending further appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from summary possession proceedings following a long-running compulsory purchase dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; the public law challenge to the deed poll should not have been struck out and summary judgment was set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Where a local authority seeks possession based on a deed poll executed under compulsory purchase legislation, a landowner may raise as a defence in private law proceedings a challenge that the authority abandoned the statutory purpose or acted outside its powers, without being required to bring judicial review promptly; section 77 of the 1845 Act can start limitation afresh, but only if the deed poll is valid.
legal_issues: Whether the Limitation Act 1980 barred the council's possessory claim after adverse possession from 1966
Whether execution of a deed poll after payment into court created a fresh cause of action
Whether abandonment of the compulsory purchase purpose invalidated the deed poll
Whether a public law challenge to the deed poll could be raised as a defence in possession proceedings
linked_authorities: Mercer v Liverpool St Helens and South Lancashire Railway
Clark v University of Lincolnshire & Humberside

confidence.notes: Full judgment provides detailed reasoning on limitation and public law defences. Source metadata lists many historical judges not appearing in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Nuisance from hotel drainage into neighbouring cellar upheld on appeal
key_facts: The Fawcett family owned 34 Market Place, Richmond; Phoenix Inns owned the adjoining Talbot Hotel.
For many years foul and surface water from the Talbot's drains entered the cellar of No 34, causing damp, smell, and loss of rent.
HHJ Moir found nuisance, granted an injunction, and awarded damages for past and future repairs and rent loss.
Phoenix appealed on alleged failures of fact-finding, knowledge, causation, and the form of the injunction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from county court judgments on liability and damages in a private nuisance claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's findings on liability, damages, and the injunction were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: An appellate court should not upset a trial judge's nuisance decision where, read in context, the judgment contains adequate findings that water originated from the defendant's land, that the defendant knew or ought to have known of the escape, and that reasonable remedial works could prevent continuing nuisance; counsel should raise deficiencies in findings or order wording at trial.
legal_issues: Whether the judge made sufficient findings on the source of water ingress
Whether Phoenix knew or ought to have known of the nuisance
Whether the injunction was too vague
Whether damages were properly linked to the nuisance rather than groundwater
Admissibility of post-trial dye-test evidence on appeal
linked_authorities: English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd

confidence.notes: Facts, findings, and outcome are fully explained in the judgment. Source metadata lists Lord Phillips though Aikens and Arden LJJ delivered the appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum and Article 3 challenge dismissed after concession
key_facts: Mr Shariff, a Kurdish Iraqi from the Kurdish autonomous area, claimed asylum in the UK in December 2000.
An adjudicator rejected his asylum claim and his parallel Article 3 ECHR claim in May 2002 after a hearing in February 2002.
Forbes J granted permission for judicial review, but at the hearing the claimant conceded he could not challenge the asylum basis of the decision.
The remaining Article 3 argument mirrored the rejected asylum case and had not been separately developed before the adjudicator.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of an Immigration Appeal Tribunal/adjudicator decision refusing asylum and human rights protection.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant concedes that the asylum decision cannot be impugned and the Article 3 claim was run on identical facts without separate argument, there is no arguable basis for judicial review; delay between hearing and promulgation did not create residual unfairness where positive credibility findings did not alter the outcome.
legal_issues: Whether return to the Kurdish autonomous area raised a separate Article 3 claim
Whether the adjudicator's findings on a family feud supported inhuman or degrading treatment
Whether delay in promulgating the adjudicator's decision rendered the process unfair

confidence.notes: Short administrative judgment with clear outcome. Source metadata lists no judges though Newman J delivered the decision.

enrichment.short_title: FIOST charterparty and Hague-Visby loading obligations

statutes_considered.title: Carriage of Goods by Sea Act 1992

key_facts: Steel coils were carried from Bombay to Spain under a Stemmor 1983 voyage charterparty and Congenbill bills of lading.
Charterparty clauses 3 and 17 placed loading, stowage, lashing, securing, and discharge on charterers/shippers/receivers on an FIOST basis.
At a preliminary issues trial the judge held owners had no charterparty liability and limited bill-of-lading liability unless owners or their agents caused the damage.
Claimants argued Article III rule 2 imposed an absolute loading obligation; owners cross-appealed on the qualification to bill liability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from a preliminary issues trial on carrier liability for cargo damage.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal allowed to remove the judge's qualification so owners had no bill-of-lading liability for loading or discharge absent intervention.
enrichment.ratio: Under English law as settled in Pyrene v Scindia and Renton v Palmyra, Article III rule 2 of the Hague-Visby Rules governs the manner, not the existence, of loading obligations; where charterparty and bill terms transfer cargo operations to shippers and receivers, the shipowner is not liable for damage caused by those parties unless the master intervenes.
legal_issues: Construction of FIOST and clause 17 trimming provisions for steel coils
Whether Article III rule 2 requires carriers to load, stow, and discharge
Whether charterparty cargo-work allocation was incorporated into bills of lading
Effect of the intervention proviso from Canadian Transport v Courtline
linked_authorities: Pyrene Co Ltd v Scindia Navigation Co Ltd
G.H. Renton & Co. v Palmyra Trading Corporation

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on charterparty and Hague-Visby construction. Source metadata lists many historical judges not appearing in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: HRA s12(3) 'likely' means real prospect of success
key_facts: Cream Holdings, a Liverpool leisure business group, sought to restrain publication by Ms Banerjee, a former in-house accountant, and local newspapers.
Lloyd J granted a pre-trial injunction after closed judgment, applying a real-prospect-of-success threshold under section 12(3) HRA 1998.
The media appellants contended 'likely' meant more likely than not and that the judge could not properly have been so satisfied.
The appeal concerned confidential business information and alleged wrongdoing by Cream.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against an interlocutory injunction restraining publication before trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the injunction remained in force pending trial.
enrichment.ratio: In section 12(3) of the Human Rights Act 1998, 'likely to establish that publication should not be allowed' means a real prospect of success convincingly established, not the balance of probabilities; satisfying that lower threshold gives discretion to grant prior restraint, though relief may still be refused where the balance of rights is unclear.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'likely' in section 12(3) HRA 1998
Relationship between Article 8 and Article 10 at the interlocutory stage
Whether prior restraint requires a more-likely-than-not merits finding
Discretion to grant injunction once the section 12(3) threshold is crossed
linked_authorities: Imutran Ltd v Uncaged Campaigns Ltd

confidence.notes: Simon Brown LJ states conclusions early at paragraph 12. Much of the fact-sensitive reasoning was in a confidential judgment not fully reproduced in the source file.

enrichment.short_title: Section 117 MHA after-care duty and delayed conditional discharge
key_facts: W, a restricted patient detained after a violent offence, was conditionally discharged by a tribunal on 9 July 2001 subject to residence in suitable hostel accommodation.
Doncaster social services, as the section 117 authority, objected to Westfield House and sought alternative placements; W remained detained for months.
W claimed Doncaster unlawfully frustrated the tribunal decision, causing false imprisonment and breaches of Articles 5 and 8.
A second tribunal in March 2002 specified Westfield House and arrangements were made for his release.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court liability trial on claims for false imprisonment and Human Rights Act damages arising from delayed implementation of a conditional discharge.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the council had not breached section 117 and false imprisonment was not established.
enrichment.ratio: The section 117 after-care duty does not arise before a tribunal orders conditional discharge in a contested case; once imposed, the authority must use reasonable or best endeavours to implement tribunal conditions, but rational professional objections to a named placement do not automatically prolong unlawful detention or give rise to false imprisonment where domestic detention remains lawful.
legal_issues: When the section 117 duty arises
Whether Doncaster breached its duty by objecting to Westfield House
Whether delayed release constituted false imprisonment
Whether section 139(1) MHA protects omissions as well as acts
Availability of HRA damages for Article 5 and Article 8 breaches
linked_authorities: R v Ealing District Health Authority, ex parte Fox
R v Mental Health Review Tribunal, ex parte Hall
R (K) v Camden and Islington Health Authority
Clunis v Camden and Islington Health Authority

confidence.notes: Detailed liability judgment with clear holdings. Source metadata lists Lord Woolf CJ and Phillips MR though Stanley Burnton J decided the case.

enrichment.short_title: Murder convictions upheld despite post-trial co-defendant admissions
key_facts: Alfred Wilkins, acquitted of indecent assault, was killed when accelerant was poured through his letterbox and ignited in February 2001.
Gary Lawson and Ian Lawless were convicted of murder at Hull Crown Court; Lawson was also convicted of conspiracy to cause GBH.
The prosecution case rested largely on confessions and threats; there was no forensic link to the fire.
After trial, co-accused Chantelle Day allegedly told fellow inmates that Lawless had falsely claimed to be a lookout.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against murder and conspiracy convictions by leave of the single judge.
enrichment.ratio: A lookout who knows accelerant will be used to start a fire in an occupied dwelling can be convicted of murder on an intent to cause serious injury or death; post-trial hearsay from a co-accused about the appellant's non-participation is inadmissible at trial and cannot be received as fresh evidence under section 23 where it would not have been admissible and does not undermine the conviction.
legal_issues: Whether a lookout's knowledge supported murder rather than manslaughter
Admissibility of co-defendant hearsay under Blastland and Myers
Whether fresh evidence under section 23 Criminal Appeal Act 1968 should be received
Whether the trial judge erred in refusing to discharge the jury over Chantelle Day's diary

confidence.notes: Appeal grounds and disposal are clearly explained. Source metadata lists House of Lords judges not sitting on this Court of Appeal judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Exchangeable bonds as deliverable obligations in credit derivatives
key_facts: Nomura bought $10m credit protection from CSFB on Railtrack plc under a 2000 ISDA credit derivative confirmation.
After Railtrack's bankruptcy in October 2001, Nomura sought physical settlement by delivering Railtrack exchangeable bonds rather than the reference non-exchangeable bonds.
CSFB refused delivery, arguing the exchangeable bonds were not 'Not Contingent' deliverable obligations because of holder and trustee exchange rights.
Nomura mitigated by selling the exchangeable bonds and buying non-exchangeable bonds, then claimed sterling and dollar losses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial on construction of ISDA deliverable obligation definitions in a credit default swap.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded; Nomura was entitled to deliver the exchangeable bonds and to damages including the forex shortfall.
enrichment.ratio: Bondholder exchange rights exercisable at the holder's option for the holder's benefit do not make principal repayment 'subject to any contingency' within the ISDA 'Not Contingent' definition; in a credit-event context those rights are commercially otiose, so vanilla convertibles may be delivered in physical settlement.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'Not Contingent' in ISDA Section 2.18(b)(vii)
Whether exchange rights in vanilla convertibles prevented physical delivery
Effect of trustee automatic exchange under Condition 9(d)
Quantum of damages for wrongful rejection and currency conversion date

confidence.notes: Construction issue and quantum are clearly resolved in the judgment. Source metadata lists Lord Wilberforce though Langley J decided the case.

enrichment.short_title: Client account claim defeated by solicitor fraud involvement
key_facts: The Law Society intervened in Michael Wilson-Smith's practice on grounds of suspected dishonesty after large sums passed through his client account.
Mr Halley claimed about US$114,000 credited to his name in the client account as commission from high-yield investment arrangements the Society described as bank instrument frauds.
The first instance judge dismissed Halley's claim; Halley appealed on trust, assignment, and section 53(1)(c) issues.
The Court of Appeal held Halley could not claim beneficial entitlement because his claim was founded on fraudulent transactions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a decision on a claim for payment out of intervened solicitor client account funds.
enrichment.ratio: A person implicated in a fraud cannot invoke equitable jurisdiction to obtain payment from a solicitor's intervened client account as beneficially entitled to funds traceable to the fraud; where property is obtained by fraud equity imposes a constructive trust on the recipient, and assignments of beneficial interest in client account funds must comply with section 53(1)(c) LPA 1925 unless validly dispensed with.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Halley was beneficially entitled to client account funds
Whether arrangement fees were validly transferred to Tidal and assigned to Halley
Application of section 53(1)(c) to dispositions of client account funds
Whether a constructive trust prevented Halley from claiming as beneficiary

confidence.notes: Core trust and fraud issues are clearly reasoned by Carnwath, Hale, and Mummery LJJ. No formal order paragraph appears in the source text.
